bibliography.abstract: As urban populations continue to grow, rising demand for the movement of people and goods intensifies traffic-related air pollutant (TRAP) emissions, leading to uneven spatial distributions that exacerbate health and socioeconomic disparities. This paper presents a data-driven framework to identify spatial disparities in TRAP emissions and quantify the contribution of each vehicle type to support targeted mitigation strategies. Vehicle-specific emission intensities and spatial patterns are analyzed at the census-tract (CT) level, a geographic unit for statistical analysis, typically encompassing 2,500–8,000 residents. A spatial statistical approach, using image-based traffic data and Moran’s I cluster analysis, is applied to evaluate the distribution of criteria air pollutants and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (NO x, PM 2.5, and CO 2 e) across the city of Surrey, Canada. The framework generates fleet-specific, high-resolution CT-level emission allocations by pollutants, which are used to identify clusters of hot spots. These hot spots are overlaid with active transportation clusters to identify areas where TRAP exposure requires targeted intervention. The framework offers a scalable approach to integrating emissions and equity metrics for equitable emissions reductions. Among the 95 CTs included in the study, five were identified as “double jeopardy” zones, where high levels of walking and cycling activity coincide with elevated TRAP emissions clusters. Passenger Trucks and heavy-duty vehicles (HDVs) are identified as the dominant contributors to emissions within the 14 High-High TRAP tracts. Passenger trucks account for 60% of CO 2 e and 45% of NO x, while HDVs dominate exhaust particulate matter (PM), contributing 57% of PM 2.5.
bibliography.title: Compounded exposure in sustainable transportation: Identifying the spatial overlap between on-road vehicle emission hotspots and active commuting clusters

en.caveats: The analysis is limited to a single municipality and relies on census-tract level aggregations, which may mask finer, street-level variations in exposure.
en.what: This study developed a data-driven framework to map vehicle-specific emissions of NOx, PM2.5, and CO2e across 95 census tracts in Surrey, Canada, using image-based traffic data and Moran's I cluster analysis. The framework identified five 'double jeopardy' zones where high active commuting clusters directly overlap with elevated traffic-related air pollution hotspots. Within the 14 highest-emission tracts, passenger trucks were found to generate 60% of CO2e and 45% of NOx, while heavy-duty vehicles contributed 57% of exhaust PM2.5.
en.why: It provides a scalable method to pinpoint exact urban corridors where pedestrians and cyclists face the highest toxic exposure, allowing planners to target emission mitigation policies at the specific vehicle classes driving the local pollution.
